courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.contribution: RequiredYear1PPD: research literacy, academic writing/presentation, reflective goals and community engagement.

availableEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
availableEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
availableEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: AI Ethics
courses.contribution: Ethical theory, fairness/privacy/responsibility and psychological analysis of human–AI interactions directly support the human-centred AI component. This is not training in linguistic annotation or multimodal language modelling.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
availableEvidence.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
availableEvidence.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

courses.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
courses.contribution: Propositional/predicate logic, quantifiers, sets, relations and proof supply a concrete complementary formal vocabulary for analysing structure/meaning. They do not implement natural-language syntax, morphology or phonological theory.

availableEvidence.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
availableEvidence.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
availableEvidence.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science
courses.contribution: Actual R text-data handling, cleaning, joining, exploration and visualisation provide direct methods for language-data inquiry. No particular corpus or linguistic dataset is guaranteed.

availableEvidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
availableEvidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
availableEvidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.contribution: Regression/classification, validation and feature/predictor evaluation provide concrete tools for later language-data models. General prediction projects are not themselves a full computational-linguistics curriculum.

availableEvidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
availableEvidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
availableEvidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

courses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courses.contribution: Actual text classification/generation, transformers and Python neural-network implementation give substantial language-technology methods. Image/text project choice does not guarantee every student a language project.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
availableEvidence.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
availableEvidence.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.contribution: Python structured programming, collections, recursion, testing and debugging are concrete prerequisites for research computing and later text/neural models; no linguistic application is assumed in the gateway itself.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
availableEvidence.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
availableEvidence.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.contribution: Actual calculus, optimisation and dynamic modelling support quantitative learning/model analysis. Current detailed evidence is not a stand-alone linear-algebra or linguistic-modelling course.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
availableEvidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
availableEvidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.contribution: Actual interviews/observations, transcription, qualitative coding/thematic interpretation and reflexive empirical research support systematic analysis of communication evidence. This is not formal linguistic morphology/phonology.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
availableEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
availableEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

courses.name: Neurobiology
courses.contribution: Comparative brain anatomy, microscopy/cell staining introductions and neurobiological mechanisms provide a bounded neuroscience foundation for language–brain questions. The animal/welfare/regulatory focus is not specialist language neuroimaging.

availableEvidence.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
availableEvidence.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
availableEvidence.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

courses.name: Perception & Action
courses.contribution: Available description supports neural sensory processing and goal-directed action using cognitive-neuroscience/neuropsychological approaches. These are complementary perception mechanisms; no undocumented speech-perception experiment is claimed.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

courses.name: Higher Order Functions
courses.contribution: Actual attention/memory/control mechanisms, attentional-blink experiment, cognitive experimental design and research proposal complement language-processing inquiry. The detailed project is not a guaranteed language experiment.

availableEvidence.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
availableEvidence.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
availableEvidence.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
availableEvidence.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review

courses.name: Psycholinguistics
courses.contribution: Available description directly supports language neurobiology, speech production/comprehension, acquisition/bilingualism, semantics, aphasia and reading/dyslexia, with actual hands-on experimental approaches. This is a substantial direct anchor, not discounted for description-only evidence; specific EEG/ERP/DES or clinical assessment/treatment techniques are not established.

availableEvidence.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

courses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courses.contribution: Neural signalling, brain organisation, learning and behavioural/imaging/electrophysiological research appraisal prepare cognitive/neuroscientific investigation. Introductory exposure is not specialist neurolinguistic experiment training.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
availableEvidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
availableEvidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

courses.name: Social Psychology
courses.contribution: Social cognition, influence/persuasion and group processes provide specific mechanisms for context-dependent communication; critical empirical appraisal and theory-guided design support inquiry. Final work proposes research, rather than conducting it.

availableEvidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
availableEvidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
availableEvidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

courses.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courses.contribution: Actual multivariable regression, ANOVA/ANCOVA, categorical/repeated-measures designs, assumptions and R-based interpretation directly support empirical psycholinguistic study design and analysis. Language datasets are not guaranteed.

availableEvidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
availableEvidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
availableEvidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

courses.name: Medical & Health Psychology
courses.contribution: Actual medical consultation, doctor–patient/shared-decision communication, interview practice and cultural formulation contribute communication and illness-context methods. They do not supply speech-language diagnostic instruments or aphasia treatment.

availableEvidence.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
availableEvidence.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
availableEvidence.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis

courses.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
courses.contribution: Systematic review, bias appraisal, effect-size estimation and R meta-analysis supply concrete evidence-synthesis methods for behavioural/language research. Taught group synthesis is not a Groningen graduation research seminar.

availableEvidence.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
availableEvidence.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
availableEvidence.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
availableEvidence.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

courses.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
courses.contribution: Actual cognitive/social developmental theories, case analysis and lifespan interviewing supply context for developmental language questions. It is not dedicated language-acquisition/disorder training.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
availableEvidence.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
availableEvidence.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.contribution: Actual rhetorical argument, discourse types, stylistic choices, audience appeals and speech analysis/delivery provide concrete language-use inquiry/practice. The applied educational storytelling project concerns climate/community, not experimental linguistics.

availableEvidence.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
availableEvidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
availableEvidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
availableEvidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

courses.name: Style & Meaning
courses.contribution: Direct morphology/syntax/lexical semantics, discourse/turn-taking, modality, deixis and cognitive stylistics connect language choices to interpreted meaning. Textual analyses are substantial language inquiry, while systematic structural-linguistics sequences remain absent.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
availableEvidence.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
availableEvidence.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

courses.name: Rhetoric in Action
courses.contribution: Actual age-appropriate speaking, debating and storytelling instruction/coaching with primary-school partners supplies applied communication-pedagogy practice. It is not developmental-language assessment or speech therapy.

availableEvidence.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
availableEvidence.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
availableEvidence.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
availableEvidence.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation

courses.name: Persuasive Communication
courses.contribution: Actual framing, verbal/nonverbal communication, argumentation, persuasion psychology and reflective field-research diaries support language-use/context inquiry. Sustainability communication is the actual setting, not a promised clinical-language project.

availableEvidence.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
availableEvidence.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
availableEvidence.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
courses.contribution: Actual close reading of narrative, point of view, style, tone and poetic form supports the concept’s textual meaning/communication dimension. Literary interpretation is complementary and does not substitute for formal semantics or syntax.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
availableEvidence.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
availableEvidence.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

concepts.label: Language processing, cognition & communication
concepts.concept: Study how people understand and produce language. Combine psycholinguistics with cognition, developmental psychology, text analysis and research methods, and explore how computers process text.
concepts.labelReason: Psycholinguistics anchors the programme, with substantial cognitive science, behavioural methods, linguistic analysis of texts and selected language technology.
progression: Brain & Behavior precedes Psycholinguistics and later cognitive and developmental courses. Statistics precedes evidence synthesis. Programming, Mathematical Methods and introductory data science precede neural networks and text modelling.

candidates.label: Structural and theoretical linguistics
candidates.reason: Formal logic and direct linguistic stylistics receive full consideration. The current palette still lacks a sustained phonology/phonetics, morphosyntax and formal semantic sequence needed to implement this separate structural concept. This is a substantive shortfall, not a title-based rejection.

candidates.label: Clinical linguistics, neurolinguistics and speech-language disorders
candidates.reason: Actual Psycholinguistics includes aphasia/dyslexia, neuroscience of language and hands-on experimental approaches and is fully credited in the strongest provisional response. General cognitive/biomedical substitutions do not establish a further coherent, substantively distinct specialist language-disorder/neuroimaging sequence. The combined Hanze pathway also has its own programme structure; absence of a professional licence is not the rejection criterion.

stopping.assessment: One provisional response is anchored in direct psycholinguistics, linguistic stylistics and real text/neural methods, with cognitive, communication and research complements. Both additional candidate families were tested against actual course content, including description-only Psycholinguistics. Neither yields a further distinct substantive structural/clinical language sequence. Comparator progression remains unresolved; this is not final comparison approval or a target-level no-match.

comparisonAlignment: Both address language processing and experimental psycholinguistics. Groningen devotes a separate course to a psycholinguistics project.
Both examine applications of AI alongside ethics and effects on people and society. Groningen also studies language, multimodality and AI literacy.
Both support empirical research using statistical analysis. UCR applies multivariable models and experimental methods to behavioural research.
Structural, clinical and specialist linguistics gaps
sourceComparability: Material language-related work comes from explicit experimental/neurobiologicalPsycholinguistics, genuine linguistic stylistics with grammar/discourse/deixis, and text-data/deep-learning methods, supported by cognitive mechanisms and empirical research. It is not established by generic coherent psychology/communication alone. Structural/clinical specialist gaps remain real.
